title: Overcoming the blood-brain barrier with nanoparticle vaccines against gliomas
text:
Despite maximal surgery, radiation and chemotherapy, glioblastoma (GBM) remains invariably recalcitrant, and
necessitates development of new therapies. We have developed a novel FDA-IND approved agent (BB-19304,
Sayour) utilizing RNA-nanoparticles (RNA-NPs) to reprogram innate/adaptive immunity against GBM. In this
proposal, we will explore the mechanistic underpinnings of RNA-NP mediated response in murine/large animal
models before pursuing a first-in-human clinical trial.

title: Role of CNNM2 in Neuronal Mg2+ Homeostasis, Function and Development
text:
Mg2+ plays an essential role in neurobiology but despite its importance, how neuronal Mg2+ homeostasis is
regulated and how its dysfunction contributes to clinical symptoms remains unexplored. In this proposal CNNM2,
a Mg2+ transporter, is leveraged as a biologically relevant entry point to understand these questions. CNNM2
expression and protein composition is characterized in both mouse and human neurons and the effect of
disease-relevant mutations on neuronal development is determined.

title: Defining the role of lymphatic vessels in wound healing
text:
A thorough understanding of cells and molecules that regulate skin wound healing is
essential for the generation of tissue-specific regenerative therapies to effectively treat
human disease. Since the manner in which lymphatic vessels function during skin
wound healing is largely unknown, we will define how these major but poorly understood
cells function during skin wound healing. Our work will improve our understanding of the
cells and molecules that control basic skin regeneration, how lymphatic endothelium
function in this process, and will have global relevance for other regenerative tissues in
patients with lymphatic disorders.

title: Diagnostic Innovations for Pediatric Tuberculosis in Bolivia
text:
Pediatric tuberculosis (TB) continues to pose diagnostic challenges in low- and middle-income countries with
high rates of TB disease, due to the fact that children do not produce deep phlegm from the lungs used to
detect TB in adults, and because sophisticated methods used in affluent countries are of limited usefulness
due to cost, restricted availability, and poor sensitivity in children. Our team will evaluate a new diagnostic
approach developed by Dr. Tony Hu at Tulane University that detects cell-free DNA from TB bacteria in a
cohort of children with presumptive TV disease and age-matched controls children. We will also determine
the correlation between cfDNA and quantitative imaging-based TB scores determined by chest X-ray and/or by
lung ultrasound, markers that may combine with cfDNA levels to improve the detection of TB disease in
children.

title: DESTIGMA: DEtecting STIgma using Generative AI among Multisite pAtients with substance use disorders
text:
Stigma is a significant hurdle to treatment for substance use disorders (SUD), often exacerbated in healthcare
settings by implicit bias and negative attitudes from providers, and impacting people irrespective of their
demographic and social characteristics. Recent advances in natural language processing (NLP) and
generative artificial intelligence (AI) present the opportunity to actively mitigate provider stigma, particularly
their communication through SUD patient notes, and also study the impact of stigmatizing language on
patients from diverse demographic (e.g., rural vs. urban) and social backgrounds. We propose to develop a co-
pilot system that leverages machine learning, NLP, and generative AI, in a multi-agent AI architecture, to
detect and correct stigmatizing language in SUD patient notes across four sites, and to study the impact of
such language on SUD patients across the lifespan and demographic profiles to enhance our ability to mitigate
the negative impact of stigmatizing languages in treatment outcomes.

title: Develop a novel therapy with immuno- and onco-targeting dual efficacies to treat the triple negative breast cancer
text:
The current study aims to develop a revolutionized antitumor therapy with both immune- and chemo-therapeutic
efficacy to treat a broad spectrum of human solid tumors.

title: The Role of the Endothelial Glycocalyx in Sepsis-Induced Coagulation
text:
Sepsis-Associated Coagulopathy (SAC) can cause blood vessel occlusion and stroke, but its underlying
mechanisms are not well understood. This project will contribute to fundamental knowledge in the short term by
elucidating the role of the vascular endothelial glycocalyx in SAC and in the long term by introducing new model
systems for research in sepsis and similar diseases. Further, we will determine whether rapid regeneration of
the glycocalyx decreases SAC symptoms in cell culture models, which is likely to offer a strong scientific
framework whereby new prophylactic, or therapeutic strategies can be developed for sepsis patients.

title: Uncovering Epigenetic and Transcriptional Drivers of Neuroendocrine Plasticity at Single-Cell Level in Patients with Small Cell Lung Cancer Transformation
text:
Histological transformation from lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) to small cell lung cancer (SCLC)
and subsequent diversification into more aggressive SCLC subtypes, are examples of
neuroendocrine lineage plasticity, a process that promotes metastasis and treatment resistance
in lung cancer. This proposal uses 1) single-cell sequencing in patient tumors of combined
LUAD/SCLC histology and 2) functional experiments in preclinical models of SCLC transformation
to identify transcriptomic and epigenetic changes driving lineage plasticity. These molecular
drivers may identify a novel class of drug targets that ablate lineage plasticity, with therapeutic
implications in not just lung cancer but also any cancer type where small cell transformation may
arise.

title: Improving the liver transplant evaluation process: a data science-focused and team-based approach
text: Liver transplantation (LT) is the only curative treatment for patients with cirrhosis, and the evaluation process regarding whom is placed on the waitlist for this lifesaving organ is opaque and difficult. Dr. Strauss will develop a data-driven intervention that will improve team decision-making for LT listing. By focusing on this critical period of the LT process, more patients in need will have access to the waitlist and transplantation.

title: Mechanisms of Innate Immune Activation in Mitochondrial Disease Onset and Progression
text:
Genetic mitochondrial diseases (GMD) impact more than 1 in 4,000 people and are the most common cause of
inherited metabolic disorders and among the most common causes of inherited neurological disease. GMDs are
a significant medical challenge, as due to poor understanding of the mechanisms underlying these conditions
there are no clinically proven therapies exist. The aim of this proposal is to follow up on recently published
findings that innate immune cells play a key role in the pathogenesis of Leigh syndrome, the most common
childhood GMD, by interrogating the innate immune mechanism signaling mechanisms that governing onset and
progression of neurological disease in a mouse model of GMD.

title: CXCR2-mediated modifications to bone marrow vasculature in chronic myeloid leukemia
text:
Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative malignancy that makes up 15% of adult leukemia cases.
Although tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) have improved patient survival, most CML patients require lifelong
treatment due to the preservation of leukemic stem cells (LSCs) and risk of relapse. This proposal will study the
role of inflammatory chemokine receptor CXCR2 in altering angiogenesis in CML and maintaining LSCs during
TKI treatment, with the goal of identifying novel strategies for targeting TKI-resistant LSCs and advancing health
outcomes for CML patients.

title: RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT FOR CLINICAL STUDIES IN THE BLUEPRINT MEDTECH. CLINICAL STUDY PROTOCOL DEVELOPMENT. TASK ORDER 02. 06/17/2024 - 06/16/2029.
text: The Blueprint MedTech program is an NIH incubator that aims to support the innovators by accelerating the development of cutting-edge medical devices for diagnosing and treating disorders of the nervous system. The mission of the program is to catalyze the translation of novel technologies from early-stage development to readiness for first-in-human clinical studies. By providing non-dilutive funding and access to essential resources, including planning support, design and testing services, and expert consultations on regulatory and commercialization issues, the program seeks to facilitate the translation of novel technologies to readiness for first-in-human clinical studies. Its goal is to enhance patient access to safe and effective medical devices while attracting further investment from industry and government. The Medtech clinical study protocol development will support translational device applications relevant to The National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) mission to seek fundamental knowledge about the brain and nervous system and to use that knowledge to reduce the burden of neurological disease for all people.

title: AMR Monitoring to Improve Child’s Health and Mortality
text:
This project proposes to leverage a large-scale sample collection from an existing cluster-randomized trial
(AVENIR II) to study the effects of azithromycin mass drug administration on clinical outcomes, dynamics of
antibiotic resistance emergence and disappearance, as well as the biological fitness of resistant pathogens
causing disease. The project will use phenotypic methods, as well as long-read whole-genome sequencing
and short-read metagenomic sequencing, to characterize antibiotic resistance in the nasopharynx and gut of
both healthy and ill children in the community and at clinics. Findings from this study will provide insight into the
use of mass drug distribution and its off-target effects in the general population.

title: Hepatitis B virus integrations in KMT2B drive hepatocellular carcinoma
text:
Hepatitis B virus (HBV)-driven hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is among the most deadly cancers worldwide
and disproportionally affects minority groups and immigrants in the US. We found 10% of HBV+ HCC tumors
carry clonal integrations of HBV sequences in the KMT2B gene within the cancer genome, which affect about
35,000 HCC cases yearly. This project will investigate this understudied oncogenic event, discover how these
integrations cause cancer, and provide novel targeted strategies to treat patients.

title: Optical microcavities for label-free single-molecule analysis of biomolecules
text:
The conformation of a biomolecule is a key determiner of its function or behavior. Assessing
that conformation, and how that conformation changes as a function of time, presence of
another biomolecule, or some other physical stimulus, is a nearly ubiquitous step in
biotechnology, ranging from molecular biology to pharmaceutical development to analytical
methods. This MIRA focuses on development of a new and potentially disruptive technology
whereby optical microcavities can assess biomolecule conformation in a way that is label-free,
fast, passive, requires little sample, and provides a readout on each individual molecule.

title: Mass Spectrometry Core (MASS)
text: PROJECT SUMMARY – MASS SPECTROMETRY The Mass Spectrometry Shared Resource (MASS) provides Salk Cancer Center (SCC) members with the highest level of support for their proteomic and metabolomic needs. The Director and Senior Mass Spectrometrist provide expert consultation concerning the design, implementation, and analysis of a wide range of experiments, including protein identification and quantification, identification of post-translational modifications, secreted protein/peptide analysis, untargeted lipidomics profiling, targeted lipidomics and metabolomics (including bile acids, amino acids, and fatty acids). MASS routinely provides service to 45% of the SCC members, who utilize 95% of total services purchased.

title: Nanomechanics of inner-ear hair-cell transduction
text:
The senses of hearing and balance rely on tip-link protein filaments that pull on transduction ion channels to
transform mechanical stimuli into electrochemical signals that can be processed by the brain. Mutations to the
proteins forming the tip link and the transduction channel complex have been shown to cause deafness in
humans and animal models. Here we propose to use structural and computational tools to gain insights into
how the inner-ear proteins forming the tip link and the transduction channel complex function in normal and
impaired hearing.

title: Genomic Instability in Lung Cancer: Unraveling the Impact of the APOBEC3 Family
text:
This study aims to investigate the role of APOBEC3 cytosine deaminases as drivers and regulators of genomic
instability in lung cancer. These aims will establish which APOBEC3s are crucial in lung cancer mutagenesis
and will study A3s' ability to inhibit genotoxic retroelements to limit genome instability in lung cancer cells.
Together, these data will define the fundamental mechanisms underlying A3 mutagenesis and set the stage for
future studies seeking to identify the causes of A3 dysfunction in lung cancer.

title: Enhancing Dendritic Cell Migration to Draining Sentinel Nodes to Improve Immunotherapy Response in HPV negative HNSCC
text:
Cancer immunotherapies has led to major treatment breakthroughs for many cancers, but majority of head and
neck cancer patients, particularly those with cancers caused by smoking and alcohol exposure, do not respond
to immunotherapies when immunotherapy is part of the initial treatment. We have shown that targeting tumors
with stereotactic radiation in combination with immunotherapy while sparing draining lymph nodes enhances
anticancer immunity, resulting in dramatic responses in previously untreated patients, and this response is
dependent on specific cells (dendritic cells) that recognize tumors and then migrate to specific draining lymph
nodes to coordinate immune response against head and neck cancers. The research outlined in this proposal
will examine the role of these migrating dendritic cell in immunotherapy response to head and neck cancer and
devise new treatment paradigms for treating head and neck cancer that leverage and enhance the power of
migratory dendritic cells.

title: Viral Vector Technology (VVTSR)
text: VIRAL VECTOR TECHNOLOGY SHARED RESOURCE The Viral Vector Technology Shared Resource (VVTSR) supports St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital (SJCRH) investigators who use recombinant viral vectors to advance pediatric cancer research. The VVTSR makes custom, research-grade adeno-associated viral, lentiviral, and gamma-retroviral vector preparations; assists investigators in the design and application of viral vectors; maintains a suite of viral vector plasmids, helper plasmids, and reagents; and facilitates the transfer of clinically relevant viral vectors to the Children’s GMP, LLC, located on the SJCRH campus. The Children’s GMP, LLC, manufactures cell and gene therapy products in support of SJCRH clinical trials. The laboratory is directed by Robert Throm, PhD, who oversees viral vector production, consultation, and development efforts. Throm earned his doctorate degree in microbiology and immunology and has worked in the VVTSR for 20 years, serving as Director for the last 5 years. The VVTSR is staffed by seven additional laboratory members, including one Managing Senior Scientist, one Scientist, one Laboratory Supervisor, three Lead Researchers, and one Researcher. In 2019, the VVTSR became an institutional shared resource, and over the last 4 years, experienced an average annual growth rate of 29% in service requests from investigators. During FY2024, the VVTSR delivered >1,000 viral vector preparations to 61 laboratories across 20 departments at SJCRH. This includes preparations for 44 St. Jude Comprehensive Cancer Center (SJCCC) members within the Cancer Biology, Developmental Biology and Solid Tumor, Hematological Malignancies, and Neurobiology and Brain Tumor Programs. Over the project period, the VVTSR has contributed to 21 publications from SJCCC members, 12 (57%) of which were published in high- impact journals (impact factor >10). These included collaborative efforts with SJCCC members to develop lentiviral vectors expressing novel chimeric antigen receptors for T-cell immunotherapy. Additionally, VVTSR worked with several members to improve viral vector production; these technological advances have been implemented by the Children’s GMP, LLC, in their clinical manufacturing of viral vectors that support multiple clinical trials for cancer and monogenic diseases. The VVTSR has also recently developed a novel Cas9- containing, virus-like particle system for editing chimeric antigen receptor–expressing T cells that will soon be transferred to the Children’s GMP, LLC, for clinical use. The VVTSR supports SJCCC members at the fundamental and translational research levels.
